item.title: Strategy and Aesthetics
item.content:encoded:
René Wiedner, Warwick Business School

Jennifer Whyte, University of Sydney

Saku Mantere, McGill University

Robin Holt, University of Bristol

Marie-Léandre Gomez, ESSEC Business School

There is broad recognition that organizational life cannot be fully understood or managed through rationalist frameworks. Scholars across the social sciences, including human geography and cultural theory, have long acknowledged how sensory experience, emotion, affect and embodied practice shape organization. Strategy studies are also beginning to understand how strategically significant phenomena–organizational routines, capabilities and identity, investment allocation and judgment, leadership, environmental adaptation–refuse to be confined to, and by, rational, logically structured analyses.

There is an aesthetic aspect to all strategy–it is as much vision as it reason; as much inspiration as analysis. Emotions, feelings, intuitions, desires and instincts can all have strategically significant influence. The symbolic and material dimensions of organising, alongside questions of purpose and structure across multiple human practices and fields, are all factors for which a successful strategic design must take account. The discursive, ecological and commercial forces to which organizations are adapting continually are encountered in aesthetic terms.

Appel publié par Strategic Organization. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • The aesthetic qualities of strategy work: combining creative expression with analytical rigor; the coexistence of, and interplay between, poetics and reason
  • Aesthetically-infused experiences such as awe in understanding how strategic organizations resist the disenchantment of strategy work through over-rationalization
  • Studies of strategy confronting cultural landscapes encouraging the production and consumption of styles rather than goods, posing complex strategic identity choices across audiences with different stylistic preferences and evaluation criteria
  • How the strategic organization of affective forces is often caught in a fundamental ambiguity between instrumental organization and unmanageable reorganization of experience
  • Examinations of analogue and digital strategic devices and how these contribute to the performance of strategic styles, including strategy work in boardrooms and informal organizing contexts
  • Investigations of the strategic appropriation of artistic activity and how organizations draw from artistic practices to reinvent themselves and maximize profitability
  • Studies of organizational design and the formation of capabilities and identities that can be structured to elicit strategically significant commitments amongst stakeholders
  • Inquiries of processual forming and formation in strategy, invoking vitalist and new materialist philosophy and questions about organizational forms
  • Engagements with the raw material of strategy in formation, including how information and data have aesthetic forms and dimensions
  • Connecting strategy and temporality through aesthetics, including how strategy forms narrative plots that elicit specific feelings of progression, symbolic and communal attachments, and identities

item.title: Strategizing in a Fractured World: MNE Responses to Fragmented Stakeholder and Institutional Pressures
item.content:encoded:
Srividya Jandhyala, École Supérieure des Sciences Économiques et Commerciales

Vera Kunczer, Copenhagen Business School

Jonas Puck, Vienna University of Economics and Business

Harald Puhr, Universität Innsbruck

Michael Wolfesberger, Vienna University of Economics and Business

Firms and policymakers are struggling to address a seemingly 'perfect storm' of political, social and economic disruptions. Rising national security concerns, populist politics, and societal pressures have produced fragmentation, i.e., the coexistence of overlapping, conflicting, or weakly coordinated rules and pressures across national, supranational, and societal spheres. MNEs must navigate the triality of home, host, and supranational institutions in cross-border business. For example, multilateral frameworks that could shape MNE sustainability initiatives, such as the UN SDGs and the Paris Agreement, face domestic resistance in some countries and are part of the legal basis in others. Such tensions between supranational frameworks and nationalist movements or policies can create conflicting institutional logics and institutional schisms. While international institutions shape firms' assessments of their domestic environments, in adapting to these fractured environments, MNEs may also amplify institutional pluralism through local responses.

Appel publié par Management International Review. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • What drives the exposure of MNEs to institutional fragmentation and fracturing?
  • When and how do MNEs integrate market- and non-market strategies across global markets in response to fragmented stakeholder and institutional pressures?
  • How do MNEs manage and organize their response strategies across different markets?
  • How do institutional fragmentation and geopolitical tensions shape interactions within firms?
